sections.html:
Jasper County is South Carolina's southernmost county, in the Lowcountry, with Ridgeland as the seat and Hardeeville as the largest community. Population rose from 20,678 in 2000 to 28,791 in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 38,533. Most of the recent growth is around Hardeeville, where planned communities along U.S. 278 and Argent Boulevard, including Sun City Hilton Head, added thousands of residents. The city went from 2,952 people in 2010 to 7,473 in 2020, with 16,459 estimated for 2025.

That growth brought a larger tax base and many new buyers, but also plenty of older family land, and the two kinds of property are handled quite differently when they are sold.

Three county offices split the work. Values and appeals belong to the Assessor, bills and vehicles to the Auditor, and payments to the Treasurer. Accounts that fall behind become the Delinquent Tax Collector's responsibility. You will find all of them at 358 Third Avenue, Ridgeland, SC 29936.

  • Treasurer: (843) 717-3601, with the window open weekdays from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM.
  • Assessor appeals questions: (843) 717-3620.
  • Main county line: (843) 726-7700.
  • Rule of thumb: land and houses go to the Assessor, a vehicle notice for a car you sold goes to the Auditor, and overdue bills go to the Tax Collector's Office.

The Taxes page on the county site links to online payment. Before mailing a check, phone the Treasurer to confirm the correct post office box.

January 15 is the last day to pay without penalty. For 2026 taxes paid in 2027, the Treasurer lists these dates:

Pay byPenalty startsTotal penalty
January 15, 2027January 16, 20273%
February 1, 2027February 2, 202710%
March 16, 2027March 17, 202715%

March 17 is the handoff to the Delinquent Tax Collector. State law stacks the penalty: an initial charge, a second layer on February 2, a third on March 17, then an execution. Two exceptions exist. The treasurer may forgive a penalty if a mailed payment got the wrong postmark. The treasurer must forgive it if the house was sold, the bill went to the former owner, and the buyer never received a notice in time. Section 12-45-180 has the exact wording.

sections.h2: Delinquent taxes and the tax sale
sections.html:
If real property stays unpaid, it can go to a tax sale, and the former owner then has a 12-month redemption period. The timeline the county posts under Section 12-51-40 is as follows.

  • March 17: the account is delinquent.
  • April 1: delinquent notices go out by mail.
  • Normally September: certified notices are sent on delinquent real estate and mobile homes.
  • Three Wednesdays in a row ahead of the sale: an advertisement runs in a local paper.
  • First Monday of November: the sale takes place at the Government Building, 358 Third Avenue, Ridgeland.

After the auction, anyone with a stake in the title can buy the property back by covering the taxes and sale costs inside the year: the owner, a mortgage company or a grantee. That is the outer limit for any plan to keep or sell the house. A closing ahead of the first Monday of November lets the proceeds pay the back taxes.

The whole process runs on paper and begins with the Assessor, and the clock is 90 days from the mailing date of your notice. The county's Assessor Appeals page and Sections 12-60-2510 to 12-60-2550 of the state code describe the stages.

  1. Request a conference from the Assessor in writing. Expect it to be set roughly a month out, and know that skipping it ends your appeal rights for that year.
  2. If the conference does not settle it, put a protest in writing, due 30 days after the conference or the Assessor's Notice of Action. Include contact details, a property description, your reasons, and the value and classification you think are right.
  3. The Assessor mails a written reply, normally about a month later.
  4. The next stop is the county Board of Assessment Appeals, and you get 30 days from that reply. Miss it and the new value is final.
  5. Both sides exchange evidence 15 days or more before the Board conference, with replies due 7 days or more before it.
  6. The last step is a contested case hearing at the Administrative Law Court, requested no later than 30 days after the Board puts its decision in writing.

In a year when no notice was mailed, an appeal can be filed whenever you like. If it goes in before January 15, it covers that tax year, and from January 15 on it covers the following year. An attorney, CPA, fiduciary or appraiser may act for you, provided the authorization names one specific person.

If the dispute is still alive at year end, the bill is issued at 80 percent of the protested amount, and any difference is settled afterward with interest.

A house you live in, together with as many as five contiguous acres, is taxed on 4 percent of fair market value. The application is due by the first penalty date in your first claim year. More than 72 rental days in one calendar year disqualifies the home.

A wrongful claim costs a penalty equal to the whole tax paid, plus interest, and the county keeps a page for reporting residential exemption fraud. Farm acreage can earn a 4 percent rate as well. If that land changes use, rollback taxes cover the current year and the three years before. The rules are in Chapter 43 of Title 12.

Reappraisal comes every fifth year, with a notice owed to any owner whose value changes by $1,000 or more. A county ordinance can postpone new values a year, so ask the Assessor where Jasper County is in the cycle.

A new roof, an addition, and electrical, plumbing or heating work all require a Jasper County building permit. Buyers and inspectors ask about this, so find out whether past work on your house was permitted before you list it. The Planning and Building office is at 358 Third Avenue, Room 202, phone (843) 717-3650. Report code violations to (843) 547-8290.

Utility service is another thing buyers ask about. Power comes from Palmetto Electric Cooperative or Dominion Energy, and water and sewer from the Town of Ridgeland or the Beaufort-Jasper Water and Sewer Authority.

The Jasper County Register of Deeds lists a $15 recording fee for a deed, plus documentary stamps where they apply. Fees became flat amounts on August 1, 2019, so call (843) 717-3615 for the current numbers.

  • Mortgage: $25.
  • Plat: $25.
  • Release, satisfaction or discharge: $10.
  • Easement: $25 plus stamps.

The state deed fee is $1.85 per $500 of value under Title 12, Chapter 24. The register's office is at 358 Third Avenue, and its mailing box number should be confirmed by phone before you send anything.

A tax debt is no barrier to selling. Obtain a payoff from the Treasurer or Tax Collector and pass it to the title company, which settles with the county before you are paid.

When the account is already delinquent, aim to close before the first Monday of November. After the sale, the clock for redemption runs 12 months. A buyer paying cash can move faster than one waiting on a loan, which helps when time is short.

For a family property, check who is on the recorded deed, and have estate documents ready if an owner has died. Questions about whether earlier work was permitted can go to the Planning and Building office.

faqs.q: What is the last penalty-free day for Jasper County tax?
faqs.a: January 15. The Treasurer lists a 3 percent penalty from January 16, 10 percent from February 2 and 15 percent from March 17, and then files go to the Delinquent Tax Collector.

faqs.q: Who takes appeals of a Jasper County assessment?
faqs.a: The Assessor, at the appeals line (843) 717-3620. Your written objection is due 90 days after the notice was mailed.

faqs.q: What is the redemption period after a Jasper County tax sale?
faqs.a: One year from the date of the sale. Paying the overdue taxes and costs within that year lets the owner, a mortgage company or a grantee take the property back.

faqs.q: Where and when is the Jasper County tax sale held?
faqs.a: It takes place the first Monday of November at 358 Third Avenue, Ridgeland. The newspaper ad gives the date and time.

faqs.q: If I owe back taxes, can I still sell my Jasper County house?
faqs.a: Yes. Closing day takes care of it, because the title company pays the county from your proceeds. Get a payoff figure from the Treasurer or Tax Collector before choosing a date.
